title: Porto in 3 days: Ribeira, port cellars and the Douro
author: Matt
intro: Three days in Porto gives you one day for the old town and its tiled churches, one for the river, the bridges and the port cellars, and one for a day trip up the Douro Valley or out to the beach at Foz. Here's how to fit it together.
seo_title: Porto in 3 days: a day-by-day plan (2026)
seo_description: Day 1 Ribeira, São Bento and Clérigos, day 2 the bridge, Gaia and the port cellars, day 3 the Douro Valley or Foz. A realistic 3-day Porto plan.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
- **Day 1:** old town and tiled churches
- **Day 2:** the bridge and port cellars
- **Day 3:** Douro Valley or Foz
- **Airport to centre:** about 30 mins by metro

Porto is small but very hilly, so the distances are short and the climbs are steep. Wear comfortable shoes, and use the metro, trams and funicular to save your legs. It's on UK time, so there's no jet lag at all.

sections.heading: Three days at a glance
sections.text:
| Day | Morning | Afternoon | Evening |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | São Bento station, the cathedral | Clérigos Tower, Livraria Lello | Dinner in Ribeira |
| 2 | Six bridges boat trip | Port cellars in Gaia | Sunset from the bridge |
| 3 | Train to the Douro Valley | Wine tasting, river views | Back in Porto |

If you'd rather stay in the city on day 3, swap the Douro for tram 1 to the beach at Foz and the gardens of Serralves.

sections.heading: Day 1: the old town
sections.text:
Start at **São Bento station**, where the entrance hall is covered in about 20,000 blue and white tiles telling stories from Portugal's history. Then walk up to the **Sé**, the fortress-like cathedral, for views over the rooftops to the river.

In the afternoon, climb the **Clérigos Tower**, the baroque bell tower that rises over the city, then queue for **Livraria Lello**, the ornate bookshop with a famous red staircase. Entry is by timed ticket, and the price can be taken off a book if you buy one. Finish by walking down the steep lanes to **Ribeira**, the riverside quarter of tall, colourful houses, for dinner by the water.

Tip: book Livraria Lello for the first slot of the day. By late morning the queue stretches down the street, even with timed tickets.

sections.heading: Day 2: the river and the port cellars
sections.text:
Take a **six bridges boat trip** from Ribeira in the morning. In under an hour, it shows you the city from the water, passing under all of Porto's bridges.

Then cross the **Dom Luís I Bridge** to **Vila Nova de Gaia**, on the south bank. This is where the port wine houses age their wine, in long cellars by the river. Most offer tours with a tasting, and it's worth booking one or two. The **Gaia cable car** runs along the riverside if you want a view without the climb.

Local knowledge: for sunset, walk across the bridge's upper deck, shared with the metro, or climb to the terrace by the Serra do Pilar monastery for the classic view back over Porto.

sections.heading: Day 3: the Douro Valley or Foz
sections.text:
The **Douro Valley**, where the grapes for port are grown, is one of the most beautiful wine regions in Europe, with terraced vineyards on steep slopes above the river. You can get there by:

- **Train**, from São Bento to Pinhão, a scenic ride of about two and a half hours each way that follows the river for much of the route.
- **A guided tour**, which usually includes a couple of wine estates, lunch and a short boat trip.
- **A river cruise**, which takes a full day each way or more.

If you'd rather stay closer, take the old **tram 1** along the river to **Foz**, where the Douro meets the Atlantic, for a beach walk and seafood. The **Serralves** museum and gardens are nearby.

sections.heading: Getting there and around
sections.text:
- **Flights:** about 2 hours from London, with direct flights from many UK airports.
- **From the airport:** metro line E (violet) runs to the centre in about 30 minutes. You'll need a rechargeable Andante card.
- **Getting around:** walk, and use the metro, trams and the Guindais funicular for the hills.
- **Food:** try a **francesinha**, Porto's huge sandwich of meats under melted cheese and a beer sauce, and pastéis de nata from any café.

Porto is on the same time as the UK all year.

sections.heading: When to go
sections.text:
- **April to June and September:** warm, sunny and the best time for walking.
- **July and August:** busy but pleasant, rarely as hot as southern Europe.
- **23 June:** the São João festival, with fireworks and street parties all night.
- **November to February:** mild but wet, and the cheapest time to go.

Our [Porto guide](/destinations/porto) has the month-by-month weather.

sections.heading: Is Porto the right city break?
sections.text:
Porto is one of the best-value city breaks in western Europe, with great food and wine and a small, walkable centre. If you're choosing between Portugal's two big cities, our post on [Lisbon or Porto](/blog/lisbon-or-porto) compares them, and we have a [Lisbon in 3 days](/blog/lisbon-in-3-days) plan too.

For longer, add the [Algarve](/destinations/algarve) or [Madeira](/destinations/madeira), or browse the [holidays in Portugal](/destinations/holidays-in-portugal) page. If you can't decide, add a few cities to somewhere.party and let the draw choose.

faqs.question: Is 3 days enough for Porto?
faqs.answer: Yes. Three days covers the old town, the river and the port cellars, with a day left for the Douro Valley or the beach at Foz.

faqs.question: How do you get from Porto Airport to the city centre?
faqs.answer: Metro line E runs from the airport to the centre in about 30 minutes. Buy a rechargeable Andante card at the station.

faqs.question: Can you do the Douro Valley as a day trip from Porto?
faqs.answer: Yes. The train from São Bento to Pinhão takes about two and a half hours each way, or you can join a guided tour with wine tastings.

faqs.question: Do you need tickets for Livraria Lello?
faqs.answer: Yes. Entry is by timed ticket, which you can book online. The price can be taken off a book if you buy one.
